In fact, as I've already argued elsewhere, I believe that accepting and acting on the notion that the users of some third party sub should rightly be empowered to force the inclusion of one rule or the elimination of another rule on some entirely different sub establishes a VERY dangerous precedent.

It is the nature of liberty that liberty must be extended even to those of whose actions we do not approve. In fact, that is the exact test of one's real support for liberty - there's no challenge and no virtue in allowing another the liberty to engage in that of which one approves. The challenge, and thus the virtue, lies in allowing another the liberty to engage in that of which one does not approve.

Since this site depends on the creation of individual subs, those individual subs must possess the liberty to shape themselves however they see fit. And yes - that does somewhat ironically run into a potential contradiction to the overarching call for liberty, since that means that an individual sub can shape itself in a way that does not actually promote the liberty of the posters on that sub. But, somewhat counter-intuitively, respect for liberty must extend to allowing them to do exactly that. To act in the belief that one is rightly empowered to prevent that is to deny the liberty of those who create and maintain the subs, and such a denial of liberty is not limited to the users of an individual sub, but necessarily extends to the entire site.

It's somewhat akin to the controversial position that businesses should possess the right to refuse to serve anyone, for whatever reason they might choose. Yes - "allowing" businesses to do that invites the immediate denial of some measure of liberty for some number of potential customers, but such a denial is limited only to the reach of an individual business. Presuming the authority to disallow businesses to do that is itself a denial of liberty - the liberty of the business owners - and is necessarily a broader denial of liberty enacted from a greater position of authority, so is ultimately a greater threat to the overarching ideal of liberty.
